title: Woodenize All of It
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart uses legendary UCLA basketball coach John Wooden's famous practice of teaching college athletes how to put on socks and tie shoes to make a case for what he calls "Woodenizing": explicitly, patiently teaching even small behaviors rather than assuming students already know how to do them well. He quotes Wooden's own account of the shoe-and-sock lesson at length, then breaks down four qualities that make it effective - it's respectful (not condescending), clear (concrete, specific detail), owned (Wooden isn't shy about prescribing his preferred method), and done once, followed by relentless reinforcement. Stuart translates the coaching example directly into classroom behaviors, like capitalizing proper nouns or entering a room a certain way, arguing the same explicit-teach-then-reinforce pattern applies to helping students put forth effective Effort. The takeaway is a blanket instruction to leave nothing to chance: if a behavior matters for learning, teach it explicitly and hold the line on it afterward.
points: Uses Wooden's famous sock-and-shoe lesson to argue that even skills adults assume are "already known" benefit from explicit, one-time teaching rather than vague expectation.
Breaks the technique into four transferable qualities: respectful, clear, owned (the teacher commits to one specific method), and taught once followed by relentless reinforcement.
Directly translates a coaching anecdote into classroom behaviors - capitalizing proper nouns, entering a room a certain way - showing the framework isn't sport-specific.
Frames reinforcement, not the initial teaching, as the harder and more important half of the technique: address every lapse politely, firmly, warmly, and consistently.
quotes: One of the best things you can do to help students put forth greater and more effective Effort is to teach them exactly what effective Effort looks like for the task at hand.
Famously, Wooden would begin his basketball seasons at UCLA by teaching his college athletes - grown men of 18 or 19 or 20 or 21 years of age - to put on their socks and tie their shoes.
I think it's the little things that really count. The first thing I would show our players at our first meeting was how to take a little extra time putting on their shoes and socks properly.
But that's just a little detail that coaches must take advantage of, because it's the little details that make the big things come about.
He's respectful. This isn't a lesson because he believes his players are stupid; it's a lesson because he believes they are important.

The key with explicitly teaching small behaviors like this is that you do it one time, as briefly as you can, using modeling or note-taking to make things clear and explicit. And then afterwards, you have just one job: relentless reinforcement.
if there's a learning-conducive behavior you want students to do well, Woodenize it. Make it clear. Give it airtime.
